decision: Which approach best resolves: WF-085 must give a Digital Sales Room deployment a documented residency region. The researched evidence says only that residency is a deployment-time choice that fixes the jurisdiction of both content and engagement data, and it is silent on what happens to records that were already written when the region changes. Every record is ordinary schema-flexible JSON in one records table with a residency_region key this workflow writes, so relocation is mechanically possible. Which rule should the workflow enforce?

state.problem: WF-085 must give a Digital Sales Room deployment a documented residency region. The researched evidence says only that residency is a deployment-time choice that fixes the jurisdiction of both content and engagement data, and it is silent on what happens to records that were already written when the region changes. Every record is ordinary schema-flexible JSON in one records table with a residency_region key this workflow writes, so relocation is mechanically possible. Which rule should the workflow enforce?

candidate_solutions.restamp_in_place: Refuse nothing. On a region change, rewrite residency_region on every live record in the deployment and report the count moved. One jurisdiction always holds the room's data. A DSAR can always say which store a record is in.
candidate_solutions.refuse_once_records_exist: Treat the choice as a one-way door: refuse any region change once a single record exists. Simplest rule to state and impossible to get wrong, but leaves no way to correct a wrong region after a room has any data.
candidate_solutions.split_jurisdiction: Leave existing records in the old region and stamp only new ones. No migration work, but the room then holds data in two jurisdictions, which is the exact thing region-based residency control exists to prevent.
candidate_solutions.purge_and_restamp: Hard-delete every existing record and stamp only new ones. No second jurisdiction and no migration, at the price of destroying engagement history on a configuration change.

evidence_quotes: Residency is a deployment-time choice that fixes the jurisdiction of both content and engagement data.
repository_facts: One records table; every field lives in records.data as JSON, so a residency_region key can be rewritten on any row without a migration.
Every write goes through AuditedDatabase, so a re-stamp is one audited transaction per record and the change is traceable.
Hard delete exists and is audited; the dynamic index is removed with the row.
DSAR fulfilment must be able to enumerate every record holding a subject's personal data, and a split jurisdiction makes that answer ambiguous.
constraints: No shared file may be edited.
The feature owns one route prefix and one domain package.
A team adding a field must need no coordination.

decision: Which approach best resolves: WF-085 needs to refuse a blocking change from a role below the administrator tier. The research names the role check but not the role, and the ticket says: read the repository's own role surface rather than inventing a role. That surface is dsr.permissions, which exports normalise_role, INSTANCE_ADMIN, ROLES and ROLE_LABELS. The natural place for the WF-085 rules is the existing domain package dsr/security_governance, which already holds WF-073 and WF-075. But backend/tests/test_wf073.py walks every .py in that package and asserts every dsr import is either dsr.store or dsr.security_governance. Importing dsr.permissions from a new module in that package therefore fails that test. This branch must not edit test_wf073.py, and CI runs the whole suite. Which approach should the change take?

But backend/tests/test_wf073.py walks every .py in that package and asserts every dsr import is either dsr.store or dsr.security_governance. Importing dsr.permissions from a new module in that package therefore fails that test. This branch must not edit test_wf073.py, and CI runs the whole suite. Which approach should the change take?

candidate_solutions.inject_the_tier_from_the_feature_module: Keep the rules in dsr/security_governance with no new dsr import. require_administrator(role, action, administrator) takes the administrator tier as an argument, PrivacyEngine takes it in its constructor next to its clock, and the feature module - which is outside WF-073's guard - is the single place that imports dsr.permissions and supplies the tier. One import site, no second role vocabulary, no other feature's file touched. Cost: the tier is a required constructor argument, so every test constructs the engine with it, and the role vocabulary the /vocabulary route serves is assembled in the feature module.
candidate_solutions.extend_the_package_and_import_permission: Import dsr.permissions directly from the rules module. The dependency direction is arguably correct, because permissions is core vocabulary of the same category as store and neither imports dsr.api. Cost: backend/tests/test_wf073.py goes red, this branch may not edit it, and CI is red on a pull request that cannot fix it.
candidate_solutions.create_a_separate_domain_package: Put the WF-085 domain modules in a new backend/dsr/privacy_governance package. Nothing of anyone else's is touched and the guard stays green. Cost: two packages now cover security and governance, and the task brief says not to create a second package for a domain that already has one.
candidate_solutions.reimplement_the_role_tier_locally: Keep the rules in the package and declare the administrator tier in WF-085's own vocabulary, depending on nothing but the store. Cost: a second role vocabulary in one product, which is the exact thing the ticket forbids and the reason dsr.permissions exists.

decision: Implementation of WF-085 meets the release bar

state.change_summary: WF-085: meet GDPR / CCPA with residency, retention, consent and a DSAR path. A feature plugin that gives a deal room a documented residency region, three hard retention classes with researched ceilings, a consent gate that fails closed, and per-subject erasure that reports the residue it could not remove. Files added, none edited: backend/dsr/security_governance/residency.py (vocabulary), privacy_rules.py (rules), privacy_inferences.py (the ten recorded derivations), privacy_engine.py (the reads and writes); backend/dsr/features/wf085_meet_gdpr_ccpa_residency_retention_dsar.py (FEATURE, a router on /api/wf-085 with 16 routes, three error handlers, seed); backend/tests/test_wf085.py and backend/tests/test_wf085_http.py; frontend/src/features/wf-085-meet-gdpr-ccpa-residency-retention-dsar/ with index.jsx, api.js, primitives.jsx and a test file; orchestration/decisions/wf-085-jev-audit.jsonl. The domain package dsr/security_governance was extended rather than duplicated, which is what that package's own docstring already does for WF-075. The administrator tier is read from dsr.permissions by the feature module and supplied to the engine, so the domain package's import surface stays {dsr.store, dsr.security_governance} and no second role vocabulary exists.

declared_unverified: No browser was driven. The page's rendering is covered by 32 component tests and by the shipped headless checks against a real server, but nobody looked at the rendered page in a browser on this branch.

Contrast ratios, the 375/768/1024/1440 breakpoints, occlusion behind the navbar and keyboard reachability need computed styles from a render. tools/check_design_floor.py says so in its own docstring and did not measure them.

The platform audit retention is not configurable from a feature, so the JSONL mirror that tools/verify_localhost.py does not exercise was not read back after an erasure. The workflow reports it as residue rather than claiming it was removed.

A deployment with more than 1000 records in one collection is beyond the scan bound this build uses. The responses say scan_truncated rather than reporting a clean sweep, and no test exercised the truncated path against real data.

The three frontend suite failures above were left alone on purpose. They are timeouts in three other features' files on a contended machine, not defects found by this change, and CI runs on an unshared runner.
The whole-suite coverage figure and the three frontend timeouts were measured while three other agents shared eight cores.
state.requirements: A feature adds files and edits no shared file. All reads and writes go through dsr.deps / RecordStore / AuditedDatabase so every mutation writes its audit row in the same transaction. Payloads stay schema-flexible JSON: no migration, no typed column, the envelope untouched. The feature owns a unique route prefix with no colliding concrete (method, path) pair. Tests exist and the whole suite is green. The frontend page builds, is discovered by the glob, and meets the design floor.

criteria.false: A shared file is edited, or the guard did not actually measure a diff

claims_backed_by_measurement.instructions: Is every claim made in the evidence supported by a measurement that was actually run, rather than asserted, read off a progress bar, or produced by a check that passed on empty input? Declared limits are not a failure of this question -- they are the honest disclosure that belongs to them.

criteria.true: Each claim traces to quoted, reproducible tool output
criteria.false: A claim is asserted, or a check passed vacuously or was not run

coverage_of_the_change.instructions: Setting aside what is declared unverified, how much of the change did the evidence actually exercise? Judge breadth, not honesty: a declared limit is fine, but a large unexamined surface is not.

criteria.true: Every surface the change introduces is exercised by a measurement, with at most incidental limits declared
criteria.false: A substantial part of the change was never measured, whether or not that is declared

audit_integrity.instructions: Does this change preserve the audited-store guarantee: all writes through the wrapper, no direct database connection, no schema change outside the envelope?

criteria.true: Writes go through the audited store and the envelope is unchanged
criteria.false: A direct connection is opened, or a typed column or migration is added

design_floor.instructions: Does the frontend meet the design floor -- 44px touch targets, visible focus, a text label beside every icon, no emoji as icons, reduced motion respected -- as checked by the scripted pass?

criteria.true: The scripted design-floor pass is green
criteria.false: The pass is red, was skipped, or is on the allowlist

verdict.instructions: Should this change land on main? Weigh the balance of the questions above rather than deciding on your own: where contract_compliance, audit_integrity and design_floor are all healthy and the evidence questions show broad coverage, answer merge with the confidence that warrants. Items listed as unverified are declared context to weigh, not defects in themselves -- but a change whose coverage is genuinely thin, or which was recovered from a base far behind main and not reconciled, is fix.
